name: Emain Macha
shortSummary: Capital of ancient Ulster and seat of King Conchobar mac Nessa — home of the Red Branch Knights and centre of the Ulster Cycle.
explanation: Emain Macha was the royal seat of Ulster throughout most of the Ulster Cycle — home to King Conchobar mac Nessa, the Red Branch warriors, and the infant Cú Chulainn. Archaeological excavation has revealed a massive circular mound and enormous timber structure dating to around 100 BCE, one of the most significant ceremonial monuments in Ireland. The name derives from Macha, a goddess of sovereignty and horses, who is said to have marked out the site's boundary while heavily pregnant, after being forced to race the king's horses. She cursed Ulster's warriors to suffer the pangs of childbirth in their hour of greatest need — the curse that left Cú Chulainn as Ulster's sole defender during the Táin.
sources: Longes mac n-Uislenn (Exile of the Sons of Uisneach)
notes: Navan Fort (Emain Macha) is an excavated Iron Age site west of Armagh city. The mythological associations match the site's archaeological prominence.

name: Rathcroghan
shortSummary: Royal seat of Connacht and home of Queen Medb and Ailill — where the Táin began with the famous pillow-talk about cattle.
explanation: Rathcroghan is one of Ireland's largest and most complex royal archaeological sites, with over 240 recorded monuments across six square kilometres. In the Ulster Cycle it is Cruachan, seat of Medb and Ailill of Connacht. The Táin Bó Cúailnge opens here with the famous pillow-talk in which Medb and Ailill compare their wealth and she discovers his white bull outweighs all she owns. The Cave of Oweynagat (Cave of the Cats), within the complex, is one of three mythological entrances to the Otherworld — Samhain cattle and spirits emerged from it each November. Medb herself is understood as both a historical queen and a sovereignty goddess.
notes: Rathcroghan is a major, well-studied archaeological complex in County Roscommon. The Táin's opening scene explicitly sets it here.

name: Cooley Peninsula
shortSummary: Home of the Brown Bull of Cooley — the prize that launched Medb's great cattle-raid and the entire Táin.
explanation: The entire Táin Bó Cúailnge ('Cattle Raid of Cooley') was motivated by Medb's desire to possess the Donn Cúailnge, the great Brown Bull grazing on the Cooley Peninsula in County Louth. This was Ulster territory, protected by Cú Chulainn alone while the rest of Ulster slept under Macha's curse — the debility (ces noinden) that struck Ulster's warriors in their hour of greatest danger. Cú Chulainn fought a daily series of single combats on the peninsula's borders to delay the army's advance, buying time until the Ulster warriors recovered.
notes: The Cooley Peninsula (Co. Louth) is consistently identified with Cuailnge across all recensions of the Táin.

name: Áth Fhirdia — Ford of Ferdia
shortSummary: Where Cú Chulainn and his foster-brother Ferdia fought for four days in the most tragic duel of the Ulster Cycle.
explanation: Unable to advance while Cú Chulainn held the ford crossing, Medb finally persuaded Ferdia — Cú Chulainn's foster-brother, trained alongside him by the warrior-woman Scáthach in Scotland — to fight his closest friend. Their combat lasted four days with increasing grief on both sides; they sent each other food and medicine across the water each night. On the fourth day Cú Chulainn used the gáe bulga — a barbed spear thrown underwater with his foot, the one weapon Ferdia couldn't defend against. Cú Chulainn wept over Ferdia's body: 'All playing, all sport, until Ferdia came to the ford.' The town of Ardee preserves the name (Baile Átha Fhirdia).
notes: Ardee (Baile Átha Fhirdia) preserves the name of the ford. The exact location within the river is approximate. One of the most celebrated passages in Irish literature.

name: Dún Dealgan
shortSummary: Cú Chulainn's stronghold in the plain of Muirthemne — his home territory that he defended alone during the great cattle-raid.
explanation: Dún Dealgan was the fortress of Cú Chulainn in the Plain of Muirthemne (Mag Muirthemne), the broad coastal plain of County Louth between Dundalk and the Cooley Peninsula. This was his particular territory to defend, and it was here that much of the Táin's defensive action played out — Cú Chulainn's series of single combats, his wounding, his magical recovery. Traditionally associated with the mound at Castletown, Dundalk (now Castletown Mount). The town of Dundalk preserves elements of the name's tradition.
notes: Traditional identification with the Dundalk area. Exact location of the fortress is not archaeologically confirmed.

name: Knocknarea
nameIrish: Cnoc na Ré (Hill of the Kings or Moon)
shortSummary: A dramatic quartzite mountain above Sligo Bay, topped by a massive unexcavated cairn traditionally known as Medb's grave.
explanation: Knocknarea rises dramatically from the Sligo coast and is topped by Miosgán Méadhbha (Medb's Lump), a massive Neolithic passage tomb cairn measuring 55 metres in diameter and 10 metres high. It has never been excavated. Local tradition associates it with the burial place of Queen Medb of Connacht. The mountain is visible from most of Sligo and would have been a commanding presence in any mythological geography of the west. W.B. Yeats wrote of it repeatedly, and is himself buried in its shadow at Drumcliffe.
notes: The cairn's Medb association is traditional rather than explicit in early Ulster Cycle texts. The cairn itself is Neolithic (c. 3500 BCE), predating the Ulster Cycle mythology.

name: Slieve Gullion
nameIrish: Sliabh gCuilinn (Mountain of the Steep Slope)
shortSummary: The mythologically charged ring-dyke mountain where the boy Sétanta earned the name Cú Chulainn — the Hound of Culann.
explanation: Slieve Gullion has one of Ireland's most dramatic geological formations — a ring of hills encircling a central mountain, with a lake at the summit (South Lake, 573m). In Ulster Cycle tradition, the smith Culann held a feast here where the boy Sétanta, arriving late, killed Culann's fierce hound to save himself. In recompense, he offered to guard the smith's forge in the dog's place until a new dog could be trained — and was given the name Cú Chulainn (Hound of Culann) for this act. The summit passage tomb dates to c. 3500 BCE.
sources: Macgnímartha Con Culainn (The Boyhood Deeds of Cú Chulainn)
notes: Real mountain in Co. Armagh. The ring-dyke geology and summit lake are verified. Also associated with the Fenian Cycle (the Cailleach of Slieve Gullion enchants Fionn).

name: Cave of the Cats
shortSummary: Ireland's most famous Otherworld entrance — a narrow cave at Rathcroghan where the Morrígan's cattle, the supernatural cats, and the howling of Samhain emerge.
explanation: Oweynagat is a narrow limestone passage at Rathcroghan — about one metre tall and 35 metres long. In Irish tradition it is one of three doorways to the Otherworld (Tech Duinn and Cnoc Áine are the others). On Samhain (1 November), supernatural cattle were said to emerge from this cave, as were the Morrígan herself and flocks of spectral birds. The cave bears a Gaulish-Ogham inscription at its entrance reading 'VRAICCI MAQI MEDVVI' — a personal name whose meaning and owner remain debated. It has been called 'Ireland's Hell Gate' since early medieval times.
notes: Real cave, fully documented. Coordinates are approximately 100m south of the main Rathcroghan mound. The Ogham inscription is verified and studied.

name: Cú Chulainn
nameIrish: Cú Chulainn (Hound of Culann); birth name Sétanta
shortSummary: The greatest hero of the Ulster Cycle — half-divine, invincible in battle, sole defender of Ulster, destined to die young and lament it never.
explanation: Cú Chulainn was the son of the god Lugh and the mortal Deichtine, trained by the warrior-woman Scáthach in Scotland, and wielder of the gáe bulga — a terrible barbed spear thrown underwater with his foot. In the Táin he single-handedly defended Ulster against Medb's entire army for months, fighting daily single combats while the rest of Ulster slept under Macha's curse. His battle-frenzy (riastradh) was so violent that his own body contorted — hair standing on end, one eye sucking inward, the other bulging out, heat radiating from him. He died young, propped against a standing stone so he would die on his feet, still fighting — a crow landing on his shoulder was the first sign he had died.
sources: Aided Con Culainn (The Death of Cú Chulainn)
notes: Positioned in the plain of Muirthemne, his home territory. The hero's divine parentage (son of Lugh) is consistent across all sources.

name: Queen Medb
shortSummary: Queen of Connacht — sovereignty goddess, military commander, and the driving intelligence behind the great cattle-raid that consumed a generation of Irish heroes.
explanation: Medb is one of the most powerful and complex female characters in Celtic literature. She is simultaneously a historical queen (several Connacht queens bore this name), a sovereignty goddess (kings of Connacht symbolically 'mated' with her to gain legitimacy), and the primary antagonist of the Táin. The epic begins with her pillow-talk with Ailill — in which she discovers his white bull outweighs all her wealth — and she immediately resolves to get the Brown Bull of Cooley at any cost. She fought on horseback herself, she bribed, she threatened, she offered her daughter Finnabair, and she ultimately broke the Fenian convention of single combat when she saw it suited Cú Chulainn. She was her own person entirely.
notes: Positioned at Rathcroghan, her seat. Her grave is traditionally on Knocknarea. Her sovereignty-goddess function is argued by scholars alongside her narrative role.

name: Ailill mac Máta
shortSummary: King of Connacht and Medb's husband — his superior white bull inadvertently triggered the Táin, and he paid for that parity with years of war.
explanation: Ailill mac Máta is often overshadowed by Medb in the Táin, but he is a more complex figure than he first appears. He is a skilled king and able fighter. The Táin begins because his white bull (Finnbhennach) exceeds Medb's best possessions in value — a gap in parity she cannot bear. He is sometimes goaded by Medb into decisions he privately questions, and occasionally acts against her plans. It is Ailill who ultimately arranges the assassination of Cú Chulainn after the main campaign, using Lugaid and magical spears. The name Ailill is attested in several Ulster Cycle figures, suggesting it may be a title as much as a personal name.

name: Conchobar mac Nessa
shortSummary: King of Ulster and lord of the Red Branch — cunning and magnificent, but morally compromised by his treatment of Deirdre and his reliance on Cú Chulainn's impossible burden.
explanation: Conchobar mac Nessa was the king of Ulster throughout most of the Ulster Cycle. Politically astute and personally imposing, he maintained the Red Branch warrior class and the prestige of Emain Macha. But he is not a simple hero: he kept the beautiful Deirdre in imprisonment, planning to marry her against her will, and caused Naoise's death by false promise. During the Táin, with Ulster under Macha's curse, it fell to Cú Chulainn alone to hold the province. Conchobar is said to have died when a calcified human brain — a war trophy embedded in a sling-ball — burst in his skull in a frenzy of rage upon hearing of Christ's crucifixion.

name: Ferdia mac Daman
shortSummary: Cú Chulainn's foster-brother and equal in arms — persuaded by Medb to fight his closest friend, and killed by the one weapon he had no defence against.
explanation: Ferdia was trained alongside Cú Chulainn under the warrior-woman Scáthach in Scotland — the only other warrior to have completed her full training. A Connacht man of equal prowess to Cú Chulainn, he resisted Medb's pressure to fight his friend until she used his honour against him. Their four-day combat at the ford is the emotional and literary peak of the Táin. Each night they shared food and medicine; each morning they fought harder. On the fourth day Cú Chulainn used the gáe bulga — a weapon trained only to him by Scáthach — driving it through the only gap in Ferdia's horn-skin armour. Cú Chulainn mourned him as a brother.
notes: Positioned at the Ford of Ferdia (Ardee), the site of his death. The town preserves his name in Baile Átha Fhirdia.

name: Deirdre of the Sorrows
shortSummary: Prophesied at birth to destroy Ulster's greatest heroes — kept in isolation by Conchobar, she chose love and exile over a gilded cage, and the prophecy was fulfilled.
explanation: At Deirdre's birth, the druid Cathbad prophesied she would be the most beautiful woman in Ireland but would cause the ruin of Ulster. Conchobar kept her hidden and planned to marry her. She fell in love with Naoise, one of the Sons of Uisneach, and placed a geis on him to elope. They fled with his brothers to Scotland. Conchobar lured them back with false promises and had Naoise killed. Deirdre lived on in grief and captivity — 'not smiling' in some tellings. She eventually threw herself from a speeding chariot rather than continue. Her story is one of the Three Sorrows of Storytelling (Trí Truaighe na Scéalaíochta).
sources: Longes mac n-Uislenn (Exile of the Sons of Uisneach)
notes: Positioned at Emain Macha as her origin and captivity location. One of the Three Sorrows of Storytelling.

name: The Brown Bull of Cooley
shortSummary: No ordinary bull — a reincarnated swineherd of the Otherworld, whose rivalrous fate with the White Bull triggered the greatest war in Irish mythology.
explanation: The Donn Cúailnge (Brown Bull of Cooley) and his counterpart Finnbhennach (White-Horned Bull of Connacht) were not ordinary animals. They were the final reincarnations of two rival divine swineherds who had fought through multiple animal forms across many lifetimes. When Medb finally brought the Brown Bull to Connacht, the two bulls fought a catastrophic battle across Ireland. The Brown Bull killed the White Bull, then stampeded around Ireland distributing body parts — giving rise to dozens of place-names where those parts landed. He then returned to Cooley and died of his own exertion at the hill of Druim Tairb (Ridge of the Bull).

name: Red Branch Knights
shortSummary: Ulster's warrior elite — the defenders of Conchobar's court at Emain Macha, including Cú Chulainn, Conall Cernach, and Fergus mac Róich.
explanation: The Red Branch (Craobh Ruadh) was the warrior-house at Emain Macha. Their three houses held weaponry, armour, and the heads of enemies respectively. Key members included Cú Chulainn (champion of Ulster), Conall Cernach (who avenged Cú Chulainn's death), Fergus mac Róich (a former king of Ulster who was exiled and served Connacht during the Táin), and Lóegaire Buadach. Their heroic code — single combat, hospitality, the avoidance of geasa — is the most complete portrait of Iron Age Celtic warrior culture in any medieval European literature.
sources: Mesca Ulad (The Intoxication of the Ulstermen)

name: Táin Bó Cúailnge
nameIrish: Táin Bó Cúailnge (Cattle Raid of Cooley)
shortSummary: The great Irish epic — Queen Medb's army crosses Ireland to steal the Brown Bull; Cú Chulainn alone holds Ulster's border for months.
explanation: The Táin Bó Cúailnge is the longest prose narrative in medieval Irish literature and the centre of the Ulster Cycle. It begins with the pillow-talk between Medb and Ailill at Rathcroghan, proceeds through the army's march across Ireland and Cú Chulainn's single-combat defence of Ulster, climaxes with the four-day duel between Cú Chulainn and Ferdia, and ends with the catastrophic bull-battle. The text survives in two major recensions: the Book of the Dun Cow (Lebor na hUidre, c. 1100 CE) and the Book of Leinster (c. 1160 CE). The martial heroic world it depicts is thought to reflect Iron Age social structures significantly older than the manuscripts.
sources: Lebor na hUidre (Book of the Dun Cow, c. 1100 CE)
notes: Positioned midway along the army's march route (Co. Westmeath/Longford area). The text is the foundational document of the Ulster Cycle.
